title: The Two Friends
summary: Two childhood companions test their bond when one becomes a wealthy minister and the other remains a poor scholar. Birbal illustrates the sacred law of loyalty.
full_text:
Two young men, Madhav and Keshav, grew up in the same village, studying under the same village teacher and sharing every crust of bread. As adults, their fortunes diverged sharply: Madhav's brilliant mind earned him a position as a senior scribe in the imperial administration, amassing wealth and a fine mansion, while Keshav remained in his village, caring for his ailing parents as an impoverished scholar.

Years passed. When drought ruined Keshav's crops and his family faced starvation, he traveled to Agra to seek his old friend's help.

Arriving at Madhav's grand mansion, Keshav was dressed in patched clothes and worn sandals. When Madhav saw his childhood friend at the gate, he did not turn away or feel embarrassed. He ran down the marble steps, embraced Keshav with tears of joy, brought him into his home, and washed his dusty feet with his own hands!

For two weeks, Madhav treated Keshav like royalty, introducing him to scholars and providing him with fine robes.

When Keshav prepared to return home, Madhav handed him a sealed wooden casket, saying: 'Brother, accept this small gift of our childhood love. Do not open it until you reach your home.'

When Keshav reached his village and opened the casket before his wife, he found it filled to the brim with one thousand gold mohurs and a deed for fertile land!

Deeply moved, Keshav wrote a letter to Emperor Akbar, praising Madhav's loyalty and stating: 'Your Majesty, an empire is blessed when its ministers possess hearts as pure as gold.'

Akbar read the letter in court and turned to Birbal: 'Is it not rare for a wealthy man to honor a poor friend with such selfless love?'

Birbal replied with profound warmth:

'Sire, gold tests character, and adversity tests friendship. Many men have friends when their tables are laden with wine and feasts. But he who remembers the companion of his humble youth, and shares his prosperity with dignity without humiliating his brother, is the true nobleman of humanity.'

Akbar summoned both Madhav and Keshav to court, praised their noble bond, and appointed Keshav head of the imperial library, reminding his courtiers that true loyalty is the rarest jewel in the world.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Two Friends"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.

Imagine an alternate peaceful ending or a new creative adventure for these characters.
